summary: Tractate Yoma daf 80b covers: The eating measure (a date) is fixed for everyone while the drinking measure (a cheekful) is relative to each person, and the larger impurity measure is only rabbinic; All foods combine toward the eating measure on YK; Eating to excess past satiety is exempt from liability; the same reasoning applies to overeating teruma.

display.whats: The eating measure (a date) is fixed for everyone while the drinking measure (a cheekful) is relative to each person; the larger impurity measure is only rabbinic
display.hint: Why is the Yom Kippur eating measure fixed at a large date for everyone while the drinking measure varies by each person's own cheekful, and why doesn't the larger eating or impurity measure require more than the standard half-loaf eating time?
display.title: The Fixed Date and the Relative Cheekful

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara treats 'the tradition fixes it' as a genuine answer, not a dodge: eating and drinking use different logics (a fixed amount that settles any mind, versus a relative amount that settles one's OWN mind) by design, and the seemingly lenient Torah measure survives challenge only because the larger rabbinic impurity measure it's compared to belongs to a different, less strict tier of law.
learning.memoryAnchor: Eating (date): fixed for everyone, tradition-set. Drinking (cheekful): relative to each person, since only your own mouthful settles your own mind. Impurity's two-egg-bulk measure is rabbinic, so it can't undercut the Torah-level YK comparison.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why is the Yom Kippur eating measure the same for everyone while the drinking measure differs by person, and does the larger impurity measure undermine that logic?
learning.coreTension: Between wanting a single consistent logic for every eating and drinking measure on Yom Kippur and the Gemara's repeated insistence that each measure follows its own tradition-fixed rule, even when a neighboring measure looks larger, richer, or more lenient in the same timeframe.
learning.coreMove: Rabbi Zeira presses three times on why the eating measure is fixed (unlike the relative drinking measure) even across differences in person, richness, or intent, and Abaye answers each time that the tradition simply fixes the date as what settles a mind, whatever the underlying variation. Rava then presses that the larger date and impurity measures should not fit the same eating-time window as the ordinary olive-bulk, and the Gemara answers first that mind-settling is what defines the timeframe, then that the still-larger impurity measure is only rabbinic and so cannot be used to challenge the Torah-level Yom Kippur standard.

takeaway.text: Each of these measures - the fixed date for eating, the relative cheekful for drinking, and the even larger rabbinic measure for impurity - follows its own tradition-fixed logic; a measure being larger, more lenient, or differently scaled than a neighboring one is not itself an inconsistency, especially once a Torah-level measure is distinguished from a rabbinic one.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may expect one uniform principle to govern every YK and impurity measure and treat each of Rabbi Zeira's and Rava's challenges as exposing a real contradiction; the Gemara's actual method is to hold that each measure is independently tradition-fixed, and that Torah-level and rabbinic-level measures are not comparable at all.

argumentFlow.label: The cheekful question concerns even Og of Bashan
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The earlier puzzle, that a cheekful seems smaller than Beit Shammai's quarter-log, is resolved: the question was posed even for Og, king of Bashan, whose enormous cheekful far exceeds a quarter-log. For him Beit Shammai's quarter-log is the lenient measure, so it is a genuine Beit Shammai stringency only for ordinary people.

argumentFlow.label: Why is drinking relative but eating fixed?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Zeira objects: why is the eating measure a fixed large date for everyone, while the drinking measure varies with each person's mouth? Abaye answers that the tradition fixes the date as the amount that settles the mind, whereas for drinking only one's own cheekful settles one's mind, not a smaller person's.

argumentFlow.label: Should eating also be relative to body size?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Zeira presses: is an average person and Og both satisfied by a large date alike? Abaye answers that the tradition simply fixes the large date as settling the mind; an average person's mind is greatly settled and Og's only slightly, but the date relieves affliction for anyone.

argumentFlow.label: Should the food's richness change the measure?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Zeira objects further: fatty meat settles the mind at a large date, but would the same volume of grapevine shoots settle it equally? Abaye answers that the tradition fixes the date-measure regardless: rich meat settles the mind greatly, lean shoots only slightly, but the measure stands.

argumentFlow.label: Why no longer eating-time for the larger Yom Kippur measure?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rava objects that ordinary prohibitions require an olive-bulk eaten within the time to eat a half-loaf, yet Yom Kippur requires the larger large-date amount in that same span, which seems lenient. Abaye answers that the tradition ties liability to eating within that duration, since only then does the mind settle.

argumentFlow.label: The impurity measure is larger still in the same time
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rava objects that impure food renders one impure at two egg-bulks within the half-loaf time, a far larger amount in the same span. Rav Pappa answers that impurity of the body from eating is only rabbinic, so the Sages were lenient and the comparison does not bind.

argumentFlow.label: Is impurity of the body Torah or rabbinic law?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa from his own statement deriving bodily impurity from a verse, which suggests Torah law. It resolves that Rav Pappa held it is actually rabbinic, and the verse he cited serves only as a support, not a true Torah source.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners expect the eating and drinking measures to follow the same logic, both fixed or both relative.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara holds them apart: eating is a fixed large date for everyone because that amount settles the mind, while drinking is relative to each person's cheekful, because only one's own mouthful settles one's own mind. The asymmetry is deliberate, not an inconsistency.

visualizableElements.item: Fixed date (eating) vs. relative cheekful (drinking); Og of Bashan's mouthful; impurity measure is only rabbinic

quizSeeds.question: How is the apparent problem that a cheekful is smaller than Beit Shammai's quarter-log resolved?
quizSeeds.answer: The cheekful measure was set even for someone as large as Og, king of Bashan, whose mouthful far exceeds a quarter-log. For such a person Beit Shammai's fixed quarter-log is the more lenient measure, so the case stands as a real, if narrow, Beit Shammai stringency.

quizSeeds.question: Why does Abaye hold the eating measure is a fixed large date while drinking varies by person?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the accepted tradition fixes the large date as the amount that settles anyone's mind and relieves affliction, even if it settles a large person only slightly. For drinking, by contrast, only one's own cheekful settles one's mind, so the measure must scale to each individual's mouth.

quizSeeds.question: How does Rav Pappa defend the larger impurity measure eaten within the same time span?
quizSeeds.answer: He argues that impurity of the body from eating impure food is only rabbinic, so the Sages were lenient with its measure. Therefore it cannot be compared to the Torah-level Yom Kippur measure, and the verse he had cited for bodily impurity serves only as a support.

sugyot.finalRuling: The Yom Kippur eating measure (a large date) is fixed for everyone regardless of body size or food richness, while the drinking measure (a cheekful) is relative to each person's own mouth; both are anchored to the standard eating-time span because that is what defines when a measure settles the mind, and the larger two-egg-bulk impurity measure does not undercut this comparison because impurity from eating is only rabbinic in origin.

display.whats: All foods combine toward the eating measure on YK
display.hint: All foods combine toward the eating measure on YK - you cannot eat small amounts of multiple foods and avoid liability.
display.title: All Foods Combine Toward the YK Eating Measure

learning.ahaMoment: The combination rule reveals what YK is really about: it prohibits the relief of affliction, and that relief can come from any combination of foods.
learning.memoryAnchor: All foods combine on YK: the target is satisfied hunger, not any particular food.
learning.learnerQuestion: If you eat small amounts of many different foods on Yom Kippur, do they combine to create liability?
learning.coreTension: Between the intuition that each food is a separate act and the halakhic principle of combination (tziruf) that aggregates amounts toward a single measure.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara rules that all foods combine: eating a tiny bit of each of many foods adds up toward the date-bulk, and liability attaches when the total reaches the measure. The prohibition targets the satisfaction of hunger, not the specific food consumed.

takeaway.text: All foods combine toward the YK eating measure because the prohibition targets the relief of affliction (satisfied hunger), not the identity of the food; any combination that provides that relief is prohibited.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may think each food is measured independently; recognizing that the prohibition targets satisfaction rather than specific consumption explains the combination rule.

argumentFlow.label: Foods combine, including salt and brine
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The mishna says all foods combine toward the liability measure. Rav Pappa rules meat and the salt on it combine to a large date, since people eat them together. Reish Lakish adds that brine on a vegetable combines with it, teaching that even something that merely prepares food for eating counts as food, not a separate beverage.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners assume liquid condiments like brine are drinks and so cannot count toward the food-eating measure.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara rules that brine, which prepares the vegetable for eating, is treated as food rather than a beverage, so it combines with the vegetable toward the large-date liability for eating on Yom Kippur.

visualizableElements.item: All foods combine toward the eating measure on YK

quizSeeds.question: Why does brine on a vegetable combine with the vegetable toward the Yom Kippur measure?
quizSeeds.answer: Although one might think brine is a beverage that does not combine with food, the Gemara teaches that anything which prepares food for eating is itself considered food. Since the brine readies the vegetable for eating, it joins it toward the large-date measure.

sugyot.finalRuling: The mishna's combining rule extends beyond distinct foods to food preparations: Rav Pappa rules that raw meat and the salt eaten with it combine toward the date-bulk measure, even though salt alone is not eating, because people eat them together. Reish Lakish extends this further with brine poured on a vegetable, teaching the governing principle that anything which enables food to be eaten is itself deemed food rather than a separate beverage, so it too joins the combination.

display.whats: Reish Lakish: eating to excess on YK, past satiety, is exempt from liability; the same logic applies to overeating teruma
display.hint: Reish Lakish rules that forcing food down to the point of self-harm on Yom Kippur - eating to excess past satiety - does NOT create liability, since the Torah's language of 'affliction' addresses only normal, beneficial eating; why does the same exemption logic apply to a non-priest who overeats teruma?
display.title: Reish Lakish: Excessive Eating on Yom Kippur Is Exempt

learning.ahaMoment: Reish Lakish's ruling reveals what the affliction-prohibition actually targets: normal, beneficial eating. Forcing food down past satiety harms rather than benefits the eater, so it falls outside the verse's scope entirely and creates no liability.
learning.memoryAnchor: Reish Lakish: eating to excess, past satiety, is EXEMPT - self-harm isn't the 'eating' the verse prohibits.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why is one who eats to excess on Yom Kippur - forcing food down past satiety - exempt from liability, and why does the same reasoning apply to a non-priest who overeats teruma?
learning.coreTension: Between assuming any act of eating on Yom Kippur incurs liability and Reish Lakish's ruling that eating to the point of self-harm falls outside the prohibition entirely.
learning.coreMove: Reish Lakish rules that one who eats to excess on Yom Kippur - forcing food down past satiety - is exempt, because the verse speaks of a soul 'afflicted,' and one who harms rather than benefits himself by such eating is excluded from that language. Rabbi Yirmeya, in Reish Lakish's name, extends the same logic to teruma: a non-priest who overeats teruma to excess pays the principal but not the added fifth, since 'if a man eat' addresses normal eating, not self-harm - though he still repays the principal because the priest suffered a real loss.

takeaway.text: Eating to excess on Yom Kippur - forcing food down past the point of satiety - is exempt from liability, because the prohibition's 'affliction' language addresses only normal, beneficial eating, not self-harm; the same exemption logic reduces, but does not eliminate, liability for a non-priest who overeats teruma.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume any eating on Yom Kippur triggers full liability regardless of manner; Reish Lakish's ruling shows that eating to the point of self-harm falls outside the prohibition's scope entirely, exempting rather than aggravating liability.

argumentFlow.label: Excessive eating on Yom Kippur is exempt
argumentFlow.speaker: Reish Lakish
argumentFlow.text: Reish Lakish rules that one who eats to excess on Yom Kippur, forcing food down past satiety, is exempt, because the verse speaks of a soul 'afflicted' and one cut off for not being afflicted, which excludes one who harms rather than benefits himself by such eating.

argumentFlow.label: The same principle applied to teruma
argumentFlow.speaker: Reish Lakish
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Reish Lakish applies the principle to teruma: a non-priest who eats teruma to excess pays the principal but not the added fifth, since the verse 'if a man eat' excludes one who harms himself rather than eats normally. He still pays the principal because the priest suffered a loss.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners assume any eating on Yom Kippur, however done, incurs the full penalty.
misconceptions.correction: Reish Lakish exempts eating done to excess that harms the eater, because the Torah's language of 'affliction' targets normal, beneficial eating. The same logic exempts the added fifth for one who overeats teruma, since that too is self-harm rather than ordinary eating.

visualizableElements.item: Reish Lakish's exemption for excessive eating on Yom Kippur, extended to overeating teruma

quizSeeds.question: Why is one who eats to excess on Yom Kippur exempt from liability?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the prohibition is framed as failing to be 'afflicted,' and eating past satiety to the point of harming oneself is not the normal, enjoyable eating the verse addresses. One who forces food down beyond fullness is harming himself, not benefiting, so he is excluded.

quizSeeds.question: How does Reish Lakish's principle carry over to a non-priest who eats teruma excessively?
quizSeeds.answer: Such a person pays the principal but not the added fifth. The verse 'if a man eat' refers to normal eating and excludes one who harms himself by overeating, so the penalty fifth does not apply, though he still repays the principal because the priest suffered a real loss.

sugyot.finalRuling: One who eats to excess on Yom Kippur, forcing food down past the point of satiety, is exempt from liability, since the prohibition's 'affliction' language addresses only normal, beneficial eating; the same reasoning exempts the added-fifth penalty, though not the principal, for a non-priest who overeats teruma.
